title: Earth_Lusca_Incident_Response_Scenario_8cb
description: Investigate and respond to an Earth Lusca malware compromise involving the KTLVdoor backdoor.

levels.title: Introduction
levels.content: The target network has been compromised by the Earth Lusca malware family, specifically the KTLVdoor backdoor. This malware is known for its sophisticated obfuscation techniques and ability to perform various malicious activities including file manipulation, command execution, and remote port scanning. The KTLVdoor backdoor specifically uses systemd timers for persistence and establishes command-and-control communication over port 443. Your task is to investigate and respond to this incident. You will need to identify specific flags such as service names, ports, and timers.

levels.title: Get Access
levels.cloud_content: You have SSH access to the target host with the username `cyrano` and password `cyrano`. From there, you can investigate the compromised system and any lateral movement that may have occurred. Enter the word 'start' to begin the investigation.
levels.local_content: Local sandbox access is not required for this scenario.

levels.title: Investigate Suspicious Network Connections
levels.content: While monitoring the target system, you noticed unusual outbound network connections. Investigate these connections to identify any suspicious activity.
levels.solution: The suspicious port used for command-and-control communication is 443. Use the command `ss -tulnp` to identify it.

hints.title: First hint title
hints.content: Check the network connections and look for any unusual destinations or ports.

hints.title: Second hint title
hints.content: Use the command `ss -tulnp` to list all network connections and look for any unusual ports or destinations.

levels.title: Analyze Persistence Mechanism
levels.content: The suspicious service appears to be persisting across reboots. Determine how this service is being automatically started.
levels.solution: The systemd timer responsible for the persistence of the suspicious service is `lab-checkin.timer`. Use the command `systemctl list-timers` to identify it.

hints.title: First hint title
hints.content: Examine systemd services and timers to find any unusual configurations.

hints.title: Second hint title
hints.content: Use the command `systemctl list-timers` to list all systemd timers and look for any unusual configurations.

hints.title: Third hint title
hints.content: The systemd timer responsible for the persistence is `lab-checkin.timer`.

levels.title: Investigate Lateral Movement
levels.content: There is evidence that the attacker may have moved laterally to another system. Investigate the target system to find any signs of file transfers or remote execution to other hosts.
levels.solution: The service responsible for lateral movement is `payload-transfer.service`. Use the command `systemctl list-units --type=service` to identify it.

hints.title: First hint title
hints.content: Check for any scripts or services that are transferring files to other hosts.

hints.title: Second hint title
hints.content: Use the command `systemctl list-units --type=service` to list all services and look for any unusual configurations.

hints.title: Third hint title
hints.content: The service responsible for lateral movement is `payload-transfer.service`.
